en: Chandomañjarī:
"Prabhā" and "Rucirā," accompanied by Sanskrit and Hindi commentaries;
First Fascicle.
Having bowed to the Lord Gopāla, Gaṅgādāsa—the son of Vaidya Gopāladāsa and the son of Saṃtoṣā—composes this work on prosody. 1.

We bow to that reality whose nature is consciousness, which manifests as the world even while remaining undivided within a single fragment; which possesses an inconceivable existence; which shines solely as its own self; and for which the Veda is the sole authority. 1.
Having prostrated before our two parents—the illustrious and wise Haridatta Śāstrī, the preeminent scholar, and Śaṅkaradeva Śāstrī—we compose this beautiful commentary named *Prabhā*. (2)

*Prabhā*: Homage to the destroyer of obstacles! Preceded by an auspicious invocation in the form of salutation to his chosen deity (*iṣṭadevatā*), the author of the work sets forth the subject matter he intends to explain, beginning with the words "The God... The poet Gaṅgādāsa—born of a lineage of physicians (*vaidya*), born from one named Gopāladāsa, the son of a woman named Santoṣā, and the offspring of the physician Gopāladāsa—having bowed down to and performed prostration before the God, his chosen deity, namely Gopāla, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, composes this *chandas*, that is, the science of prosody.

O Śaṅkara, you who possess stainless intellect, who grant excellent power, who bestow happiness, the crest-jewel of those of great fame, and who have given [this] to me; O Madhukara of the mind, your lotus feet are the delight of Haridatta.
O Śrīśa, Īśa, Jagadīśa, victory, victory, victory to you, O source of compassion!
O Lord, make this "Rucirā" tilaka fruitful—beautiful, radiant, and boundless.
Although there exist many Chāndoga texts for the wise, nevertheless, having extracted the essence, this effort of mine is for the sake of a new exposition. ||2||

Objection: "But surely, since there already exist the *Chandaḥsūtra* and other works composed by the ornaments of the assembly of poets such as Piṅgala, what is the purpose of this labor? To dispel this doubt, he says: "They exist," and so forth. Although many (*bhūyāṃsaḥ*) treatises on prosody (*chandogranthāḥ*) exist—that is, are found—among the learned ancient teachers (*manīṣiṇāṃ pūrvācāryāṇām*) such as Piṅgala and others, nevertheless, even while those exist, my effort (*udyamaḥ*), namely my labor (*śramaḥ*), for the sake of a new purpose—the instruction of children—is present; [the ellipsis is] "it exists. This effort belongs to me, Gaṅgādāsa, having extracted and compiled the essence (*sāram*), that is, the portion of the truth, from Piṅgala and the others.
This lovely Mañjarī of meters, rich with the pastimes of Acyuta, possessing good conduct and noble birth, will cling to the throats of the refined. (3)

[Objection: But surely, since this work is intended for the instruction of beginners, what is its purpose for the learned? To this he says: "This *Acyuta*... and so forth. This [work], which is about to be described, is rich in the pastimes of Acyuta (Śrī Kṛṣṇa) and charming with His amorous sports; it is composed in good meters (*sadvṛtta*), being surrounded by captivating verses; it is distinguished by its *jāti* meters, being delightful through verses of fixed syllabic measures (*mātrā*); it is lovely and beautiful; and it is the *Mañjarī of Meters* (*Chandomañjarī*). It will cling—that is, it will become well-established—upon the necks of the refined, that is, upon the throats of the assembly of scholars.

The intention is that the learned and sensitive-hearted will accord honor to this [work] which possesses the beauty of Gopāla’s pastimes. Here, by the word *kāntā*, a certain beautiful woman is suggested (*dhvani*). In the case of the beautiful woman, the sense is: "This *mañjarī*—rich in the pastimes of Acyuta, shining with full charm, of virtuous conduct (*sadvṛttā*), noble by birth (*jātiśālinī*), and captivating as a necklace (*hārabhūtā*)—will adorn the throat of the wise.
A verse (*padya*) consists of four lines (*catuṣpadī*), and it is of two kinds: *vṛtta* (metrical) and *jāti* (prosodic).
"A *vṛtta* is defined by the number of syllables, while a *jāti* is formed by the number of morae (*mātrā*). (4)

The author first explains what is to be explained, beginning with the word "padyam" (verse). A *pāda* is a fourth part of a *śloka*. As it has been stated: "A fourth part of a metrical unit (*mātrika*) is called a *pāda*. Thus, a *mātrika* *śloka* consisting of four *pādas*, or a set of four quarters, is designated by the term *padya* (verse). Furthermore, that *padya* is of two kinds: *vṛtta*, which is called by the name *vṛtta* (metre based on syllables), and *jāti*, which is known as *jāti* (metre based on morae). Thus, it is of two types.

That which is reckoned by syllables (*akṣara*) and calculated by phonemes (*varṇa*) is *vṛtta*, which is the name for a metrical foot. That which is composed of morae (*mātrā*), bound by short and other morae, is *jāti*, which is the name for a prosodic class. It should be known that a single-mora syllable is light (*laghu*) and a double-mora is heavy (*guru*). And likewise: "A short vowel (*hrasva*) shall consist of one mora, a long (*dīrgha*) is said to consist of two morae;
a protracted (*pluta*) is to be known as consisting of three morae, and a consonant (*vyañjana*) consists of half a mora."
Metre is of three kinds: even (sama), half-even (ardhasama), and uneven (viṣama).
The even [metre] consists of four equal feet, while the half-even [metre] is as follows: ||5||
That which has its third foot like the first and its fourth foot like the second, with four feet having different metrical marks, is proclaimed as *viṣama* (irregular). 6.

Commentary: "Equal" (sama). That aforementioned *vṛtta* is of three types—equal (*sama*), half-equal (*ardhasama*), and unequal (*viṣama*). An equal verse is one whose four quarters (*catuṣpāda*) are identical, meaning its four feet (*caraṇa*) are equal; it is the poetic meter named "equal."

That verse whose first quarter (the first foot) is like the third, and likewise whose fourth quarter (the fourth foot) is like the second, is proclaimed and declared to be a verse named *ardhasama* (half-equal). A verse consisting of four quarters with distinct marks—that is, a quartet of feet with different characteristics—is proclaimed and called *viṣama* (uneven).
By these ten syllables—*myara-staja-bhna-ga*, ending in long vowels (*lāntaiḥ*)—the entirety of literature is pervaded, just as the three worlds are by Viṣṇu. (7)

The author indicates the ten conventional groups (gaṇas) with the words "myarastajabhnagāḥ. By these—indicated as such, ending in *la* (meaning those whose final letter is *l*), namely *ma*, *ya*, *ra*, *sa*, *ta*, *ja*, *bha*, *na*, and *ga*—the entire body of literature consisting of speech, that is, the science of prosody (*chandaḥśāstra*), is pervaded by Viṣṇu, the Supreme Lord, just as the three worlds are pervaded by Him. These ten syllables constitute the complete system.
The intention is that all meters will be defined by means of these very ten syllables.

The letter *ma* consists of three heavy syllables (*g*), and the letter *na* consists of three light syllables (*l*). Furthermore, the letter *bha* has a heavy syllable at the beginning, while the letter *ya* has a light syllable at the beginning.

The letter *ja* has a heavy syllable in the middle, and the letter *ra* has a heavy syllable in the middle; that which has a heavy syllable at the end is called *antaguru*, and from that, the *antalaghu* [is understood]. (8)

The primary [commentary] defines the conventions (*saṅketa*) as follows: "ma-strī" and so forth. It should be understood that the ten syllables beginning with *ma* constitute the ten *gaṇas*, such as *magaṇa*, *yagaṇa*, and so on. *Triguru*: Where there are three heavy (*guru*) syllables, that is *ma*; it becomes *magaṇa*. *Trilaghu*: Where there are three light (*laghu*) syllables, that is *na*; it becomes *nagaṇa*. *Bhādiguru*: Here, *bha* is a nominative singular with the first vowel elided (*luptaprathamaikavacana*). *Ādiguru* means where the first syllable is heavy and the other two are light; that is *bha*; it becomes *bhagaṇa*.

Furthermore: where the first syllable is light (laghu), followed by two heavy (guru) syllables, that is the *yagaṇa*. Where there is a heavy syllable in the middle—that is, a heavy letter in the center with light syllables at the beginning and end—that becomes the *jagaṇa* (*ja*). "With *ra* in the middle": here *ra* is a nominative singular with the initial vowel elided; where there is a light syllable in the middle—that is, a light syllable in the center with heavy syllables at the beginning and end—that is *ra*, the *ragaṇa*. "Heavy at the end": where there is a heavy syllable at the end and the two preceding ones are light, that is *sa*, the *sagaṇa*. "Light at the end": where there is a light syllable at the end and the two preceding ones are heavy, that is *ta*, the *tagaṇa*; thus it has been stated and declared.
The letter *ga* is one guru, while the letter *la* is one laghu;
their respective positions are shown by lines in the following order. (9)
"Prakriyā 0—Regarding 'guru': a single syllable, *ga*, is heavy (*guru*). When *ga* is uttered, it should be understood as one heavy syllable.

A single syllable, *la*, is light (*laghu*). When *la* is uttered, it should be understood as one light syllable. The configuration—that is, the shape—of these groups beginning with *ma* is shown and made known by means of lines, which are specific marks. For example, the shape of a heavy syllable is thus (*'*) [a horizontal line], while the shape of a light syllable is thus (*1*) [a vertical line]. Here, all those consisting of four *mātrās* that are heavy at the end, in the middle, or at the beginning are to be understood."
The groups (gaṇas) in the Āryā and other meters consist of five units, each followed by four short syllables. ||10||

Now he points out the *gaṇas* of the *jāti* meters, beginning with "are to be known" (*jñeyāḥ*). Here, those accompanied by four short syllables—that is, possessing four short phonemes—and having a long syllable at the end, middle, beginning, or [all] positions—since the word "long" (*guru*) is heard at the end of the compound, it is connected to each [term]—there are five such types: the all-long (*'''), the end-long (*'||'), the middle-long (*|'||'), the beginning-long (*'||'), and the four-short (*||||'). These five *gaṇas*, consisting of four counts or four morae, are to be known as established in the *jāti* meters such as the *Āryā*.
A syllable is heavy if it contains an anusvāra, is long, or has a visarga;
likewise, it is heavy if it is preceded by a consonant cluster (saṃyoga) or occurs at the end of a metrical foot.

Now [the author] indicates the heavy syllables (*guru*): "with *anusvāra*. A vowel (*svara*)—namely *a*, *i*, *u*, *ṛ*, *lṛ*—accompanied by an *anusvāra* becomes heavy. A long vowel (*dīrgha*: *ā*, *ī*, *ū*, *ṝ*, *e*, *ai*, *o*, *au*), one followed by a *visarga* (*visargī*), and one preceded by a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga-pūrvakaḥ*)—that is, a syllable whose preceding sound is a conjunct—are also heavy. Furthermore, a syllable at the end of a quarter-verse (*pādāntagaḥ*) or a light syllable (*laghu-varṇaḥ*) may optionally become heavy.

Since this rule is fixed, it should be understood that in *vṛtta* (metrical) compositions, a syllable may be either light or heavy; however, in *jāti* (prosodic) compositions, both light and heavy syllables are considered heavy at the end [of a line]. Because the term "anusvāra" is used as an inclusive indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*), even if a consonant follows, the syllable remains heavy. In this context, a light syllable situated at the end of a quarter-verse (*pāda*) may optionally become heavy. For example: *taruṇaṃ sarṣapaśākaṃ navaudanaṃ picchilāni ca dadhīni*.
O beautiful one! With little expense, the common folk eat sweet food.
The word *sundarī* optionally becomes light when followed by a vulgar term (*grāmya*). Commentary:

He illustrates the optional heaviness of a short syllable situated at the end of a quarter-verse (*pādānta*) with the example "taruṇam. O beautiful one (*sundari*), the vulgar person—that is, a village dweller—eats fresh (*taruṇa*) mustard greens (*sarṣapaśāka*), new rice (*navaudana*), and oily curds (*picchilāni dadhīni*), all very sweetly (*miṣṭam*), with little expense (*alpavyayena*), that is, with scanty wealth. Here, the meter is Āryā.

Regarding its definition: there are twelve *mātrās* in the first quarter, eighteen in the second, twelve again in the third, and fifteen *mātrās* in the fourth. In this verse, the final syllables of the second and fourth quarters, though light (*laghu*), possess heaviness (*gurutva*). In the third quarter, the vowel *i* at the end of the quarter does not possess heaviness, even though it precedes a conjunct consonant (*saṃyukta*)—this is according to the rule concerning rusticity (*grāmya*). Thus, the meaning is that there is no violation of the meter (*chandobhaṅga*). Likewise, in my father’s play, *Pārijātaharaṇa*:

May my claws, which are like thunderbolts, enter the frontal globes of the rutting celestial elephants stationed on the battlefield— globes that possess the beauty of a face reddened by the application of vermilion and are filled with the water of the cascading streams of their constant flow of ichor.

In this verse, the light syllable at the end of the third and fourth quarters becomes heavy. Question: He illustrates the heaviness of a light syllable at the end of a quarter with the example beginning "sindūra-". This is a speech by Garuḍa, who is enraged toward Śakra. My own claws (*nakharāḥ*) are themselves thunderbolts (*aśanayaḥ*). [The elephant] possesses the splendor and luster of the red lead (*gaurika-rāga*)—that is, a crimson hue resembling red lead—produced by a mass of vermilion (*sindūra-pūra*). Furthermore, it possesses a constant and perpetual flow of rutting ichor (*mada-sravaṇa*), which is like a torrential flood of water (*nirbhara-vāri-pūra*), a mass of flowing liquid.

"Let them enter upon the frontal globe—that is, the peak or summit—of that intoxicated celestial elephant, Airāvata, who has gone to the field of battle. This is the poetic figure *ekadeśavivartirūpaka* (partial metaphor), as it is said: "That is called *ekadeśavivarti* where one part [of the object] is intended as the literal meaning. The meter is *vasantatilakā*. Here, although the syllables *mbha* and *ntu* at the end of the third and fourth quarters are light (*laghu*), they possess the weight of a heavy syllable (*guru*). Likewise, in my *Acyutacarita*: [The verse follows: *saṅgrāmabhūmigato yuddhakṣetragato yo mattaḥ surebha airāvatas tasya kumbha eva kūṭaṃ śikharaṃ tasmin viśantu praviśantu | ekadeśavartirūpakālaṅkāraḥ | uktaṃ ca 'yatra kasyacid ārthatvam ekadeśavivarti tat' iti | vasantatilakaṃ vṛttam | atra tṛtīyacaturthapādāntasthayoḥ 'mbha' 'ntu' varṇayor laghor api gurutvam | tathā mamācyutacarite 'pi —* (Note: The final sentence indicates this pattern occurs elsewhere in the author's own work.)
That staff-like arm of Hari, adorned with blood born from the wounds of Keśin, shone even more brilliantly,
as if strewn with a mass of glowing sparks from the fierce fire of his arm’s prowess ignited by the bite of that demon.
In this case, even a short syllable at the end of the first and third quarters [of a verse] is considered heavy.
Question: Regarding the word "raktena" (by the red one)—that staff-like arm of Hari (Viṣṇu) is indeed the staff of Hari (Viṣṇu), [rendered red] by the occurrence of wounds from Keśin's teeth.

Adorned most beautifully—that is, most exquisitely decorated—with the blood (lohitena) arising from the wounds inflicted by the teeth of the Dānava named Keśin; [the sword] shone, appearing as if overspread by a mass of sparks (kaṇaprakara) clearly ignited—that is, a collection of glowing embers—from the fire of the majesty (pratāpa), which is the very luster (tejas), of that formidable and terrifying arm (bhuja) of his, Keśin, which had been crushed and mangled by his teeth (daśana). The meter is Vasantatilaka.

In this context, it should be understood that the *na* and the *pa* situated at the end of the first and third quarters [of a verse] possess the status of a heavy syllable (*guru*). Furthermore, the rule "or before *pa*" (*padānte vā*) is a sūtra by the sage Piṅgala that provides an option. An example is found in the *Kumārasambhava*:
"She, her limbs purified by an auspicious bath, having taken up the garments for the return visit..."
She shone like the earth when the rain-god has finished his work, when the ritual ablution with water has been performed, and the kāśa flowers are in full bloom.
In this context, when the word *pra* follows, there is lightness (*laghutva*) for a heavy syllable (*guru*).

*Pra0-prahne vā*: the meaning is that before the word *pra* or the word *hre*, the preceding syllable may optionally (*vibhāṣā*) be heavy. However, this rule is not seen in the currently extant *Piṅgala-chandaḥsūtra*. *Sā maṅgalā*.

With her limbs purified and her body sanctified by an auspicious bath and a consecration for the sake of good fortune; wearing a *pratyudgamanīya* garment—that is, a pure white cloth—Pārvatī shone like the earth, upon which the *kāśa* flowers have blossomed, when its sprinkling with the water of the rain-cloud has been completed—that is to say, when it is drenched by the water of the clouds. The meter is *upajāti*.
In this case, the *t* sound preceding the *pra* cluster does not possess "heaviness" (*gurutva*). Therefore, there is no fault of violating the metrical rules (*chandobhaṅga*).
Having quickly reached the pool at the navel for immersion, the beloved woman seized with her own hands the hand of her lover as he was setting out to take up his upper garment.
In this case, when the word *hra* follows, there is lightness for a heavy syllable. [Commentary:

"Having reached" (*prāpya*). A certain beloved woman, with her own hands (*ātma-karābhyām*), having reached—that is, having approached—the immersion in the lake that is her very navel (*nābhi-hrada*), quickly and swiftly, for the purpose of seizing her garment—that is, for pulling at her cloth—she obstructed, she held back, the hand of her lover, which had set out—that is, had proceeded—to reach the region of the navel (*aupanīvika*). This is the meaning. The meter is *svāgatā*. Here, the vowel *i* of the word *nābhi*, which precedes the word *hra*, does not possess heaviness according to the preceding rule.
Regarding this, the *Kaṇṭhābharaṇa* states that there is lightness here due to pronunciation with intense effort (*tīvraprayatna*). As it has been said:

"When, through intense effort, there is no heaviness at the beginning of a conjunct consonant (*saṃyoga*) and so forth, and the meter is not broken, then the wise declare that it does not constitute a fault."

Pra0—Regarding the term *tīvra*: the teacher Kaṇṭhābharaṇakāra states that when there is an utterance characterized by intense (*tīvra*) or forceful effort (*prayatna*), even a heavy syllable becomes light. He establishes the settled conclusion (*rāddhānta*) of the ancient teachers—that the rule "that which precedes a conjunct consonant is heavy" is not universal—by saying *yadā* (when).

When, through reading with intense effort and rapid speed (*drutagati*), there is a lack of heaviness—that is, lightness—of the syllable preceding a conjunct (*saṃyoga*), then there is no violation of the meter; it does not bring about a fault.
The pause (*yati*) is said by poets to be the place of rest for the desired [metrical] break; it may be indicated at will by means of word-breaks, stops, and so forth. (12)

Now, he indicates the definition of *yati*: "The pause (*yati*). That which is the desired place of rest or the place of stability for the tongue is called *yati* by poets; the meaning is that where the tongue ceases of its own accord, there is a *yati*. That *yati* is to be expressed—made known—by the speaker’s own will, through terms such as *viccheda*, *virāma*, and so forth, and by means of words (*pada*).
The point is that terms such as *viccheda*, *virāma*, and *virati* are synonyms for *yati*.
In some meters, a pause (yati) has been prescribed by former masters;
it attains beauty at the end of a word but is abandoned in the middle of a word.
Furthermore, in that very same case, when a euphonic combination (sandhi) is determined by the vowels, it resumes that [pause].
Just as Kṛṣṇa, whose greatness is incomparable, may nourish me with compassion. ||13||
And this verse belongs to my teacher Puruṣottama’s work titled *Chandogovinda*.

Question: It points out a specific distinction with the words "In some cases" (*kvacit*). This verse beginning with "In some cases" exists in the work of my teacher Puruṣottama named *Chandogovinda*. The meaning is that the pause (*yati*) prescribed by earlier authors—that is, by ancient scholars—exists in some meters, specifically within the scope of prosody (*chandaḥ*), but not everywhere.

However, that pause (*yati*) which, being situated at the end of a word (*padānta*), attains or acquires beauty and charm, that very same pause, when situated in the middle of a word (*padamadhye*), abandons it—that is, it relinquishes its pleasant sound. The sense is that a pause occurring in the middle of a word is harsh to the ear. Furthermore, but in that very same place—the middle of the word—that pause, being joined with a sandhi produced by vowels (*svaravihitasandhi*), resorts to or regains that beauty. Thus, for example: "yathā... [followed by an illustration].

May that Kṛṣṇa, whose greatness and majesty are incomparable and peerless, nourish and protect me through His compassion and mercy. Here, the meter is named Śikhariṇī, defined by the rule "rasai rudraiśchinnā" (divided by six and eleven syllables). Although the pause (*yati*) should normally occur after the first six syllables, in the example given—*puṣṇātu*—the pause is difficult to hear; however, it attains beauty here due to its connection with the euphonic combination (*sandhi*) in *puṣṇātvatule*. As stated in the *Kavikalpalatā*: "In such a way that no distress arises for the wise, so should the pause be desired for the sake of sweetness."
The sense is that in whatever metrical pause (yati) the sound becomes most pleasing to the ear, that pause should be respected.
However, the sages beginning with Śveta and Māṇḍavya do not accept such a pause;
thus says my teacher Puruṣottama Bhaṭṭa in his own work. (14)

"Śveta," etc. The learned scholars headed by Śveta and Māṇḍavya—Śveta, Māṇḍavya, and others—do not desire [this], that is, they do not accept it; thus my teacher, the preceptor Puruṣottama Bhaṭṭa, says and declares in his own work. This opinion is not pleasing, because it results in the fault of a breach of the *yati* (caesura). As it is said in the *Kāvyādarśa*: "The wise know *yati* to be the division of words at fixed places in verses; that which is devoid of this is 'breached in *yati*', causing distress to the ear, as for example: [followed by an example].
A caesura must indeed be observed at fixed positions; otherwise, the verse would become difficult to recite.
For this very reason, Murāri says:
"When the enemy of the three cities was satisfied, [he whose] circle of arms was itching..."

How can that Ten-necked one be described— he whose faces, having been plucked by his sport yet grown back again, turned away from the wretchedness of begging for boons from a hero, and contended with one another on all sides, saying, "You choose! You choose!"?

"Contented," etc. This verse was composed by Murāri. It is the speech of Śauṣkala, the priest of Rāvaṇa, addressed to Janaka. "Of the three cities" means of the three fortresses; "in the enemy" refers to the foe, namely Śiva, the destroyer of Tripura.

Even though he was contented and pleased by his asceticism, [the heads] of that hero Rāvaṇa—who desired to obtain a boon—were such that their heads were cut off and regrown again and again through the playful sport of his massed arms, which were intent on scratching; thus, his faces displayed the wretchedness of begging.

With a state of wretchedness born from his prayer, those [faces] were turned away and bowed down; on both sides, they cried out, "Choose you! Choose you! and fell into a quarrel, engaging in dispute. How can that Rāvaṇa—who was thus thwarted even in his request for a boon—be described? Thus, one of such great majesty is truly beyond description. This is in the Śārdūlavikrīḍita meter; the caesura is fixed at the end of the twelfth syllable, yet in the third foot, it is not perceived at the end of the syllables *kala* and *hā* in the word *kalahāyante*. Jayadeva also says: [The Sanskrit verse follows: *prārthanāsañjātadīnabhāvaḥ tena parāñci avanatāni santi, abhitaḥ ubhayataḥ, tvaṃ vṛṇu tvaṃ vṛṇu iti, kalahāyante vivādaṃ kurvanti| evaṃ sa rāvaṇo, yo varayāñcāyāmapi kuṇṭhitaḥ, kathaṃ kathyatāṃ varṇyatām, evaṃ mahāmahimā'varṇanīya eva| śārdūlavikrīḍitaṃ vṛttam| dvādaśākṣarāvasāne yatirniyatā, sā tṛtīyapāde kalahāyanta iti hāvarṇānte na saṃlakṣyate| jayadevo'pi —* (Note: The provided text contains a repetition of the Sanskrit fragment. The translation reflects the content as presented.)
"Excellent, honey! You need have no anxiety. O sugar! You are but a pebble.
O grape! Who will look upon you? O nectar! You are but death. O milk! Your essence is but water.
O mango! Cry out, O lip of a beloved! Go to the surface of the earth," so they say, as long as [the lips] bestow [their sweetness].
May the words of Jayadeva, which consist of the essence of the *Śṛṅgāra* sentiment and the goddess Sarasvatī, pervade all directions.

Commentary: This is a verse composed by Jayadeva, beginning with "Sādhvīti. O Mādhvīka! O Madhu! For as long as, in this world, the words—the well-spoken verses—of Jayadeva, that poet overflowing with the essence of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgārarasa*), bestow and distribute delight (*bhāva*) everywhere, for that long, concern regarding yourself—that is, reflection upon your own preservation—is neither good nor charming.

O sugar-candy! You are *karkara*, you are hard. O grape! Who—those who know taste—will see you? They will look upon you with indifference; the meaning is that because you grow in an inaccessible place, you are not an object of respect. O nectar! You are dead! The sense is that no one living can obtain you. O milk! Your juice is *nīra* (water), like water, because it lacks flavor prior to being churned. O mango (*mākanda*), O *rasāla*! You, weep and cry out!
